1 big thing: Jensen Huang comeback push tests the limits of CEO power
By Ina Fried
 

Photo illustration: Aïda Amer/Axios. Photos: Kevin Carter and Jose Sarmento Matos/Bloomberg via Getty Images
 

The push to reinstate Jensen Huang is set to test whether America's most powerful CEOs can still be held accountable — or if extraordinary success and political alliances have made them untouchable.

Why it matters: Silicon Valley has long treated its most successful founders as indispensable. But a new class of tech billionaires, led by figures like Elon Musk, has amplified that culture while swatting away efforts to curtail their power.

  • Their immense wealth and growing political clout raise a fundamental question: Can corporate boards, regulators, Congress or the courts actually rein in a superstar CEO anymore?
  • Huang's potential return — or the Nvidia board's refusal to entertain it — could signal whether that balance of power is changing.
  • "Power corrupts, and people start to think they are invincible," Anne Wojcicki, the founder of 23andMe and ex-wife of Google co-founder Sergey Brin, told Bloomberg. "We are all complicit in making these people think they are gods. And people do stupid things when they think they are untouchable."

Driving the news: A growing campaign to reinstate Huang has attracted more than 180,000 signatures, including thousands of people identifying themselves as Nvidia employees, following his departure after revelations of intimate relationships involving subordinates and an alleged Chinese spy.

  • President Trump said yesterday he wouldn't mind seeing Huang return. Musk has also backed the effort.
  • Other supporters include Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Replit CEO Amjad Masad and Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke.
  • Prominent investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker have separately urged the board not to rule out Huang's return.

Some pushing for a reexamination of the issue have focused on what they see as a lack of proof that Alice Huang, the executive with whom he had an affair, was a Chinese intelligence asset.

  • That claim has been attributed in media reports to U.S. intelligence officials, although other stories have called it into question.

Yes, but: Others have pointed to the fact that Alice Huang worked on behalf of Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer that took steps to help Chinese AI companies access cutting-edge chips.

  • The company has been linked to more than $4 billion in Nvidia chip purchases and also arranged nearly $12 billion in orders of top-end Nvidia chips destined for Chinese companies, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Nvidia's board isn't currently considering reinstating Huang, CNBC and Reuters reported yesterday.

Zoom out: Musk has become perhaps the most prominent embodiment of the superstar CEO, repeatedly defying corporate conventions and weathering controversies that might have ended other executives' careers.

  • In 2018, Musk settled SEC fraud charges over tweets about taking Tesla private, stepping down as chairman but remaining CEO.
  • After a Delaware judge invalidated his enormous Tesla compensation package, shareholders voted to ratify it, and the state's Supreme Court eventually restored the award.
  • Last year, Tesla shareholders approved another potentially massive compensation package, underscoring their willingness to grant extraordinary rewards to a leader they consider indispensable.

The Trump factor: Trump's return to the White House added another layer to the power of tech executives, many of whom cultivated close ties to a president whose decisions can affect their businesses through government contracts, regulation and trade policy.

  • But this month's midterm elections demonstrated limits to Trump's political power, raising questions about whether his backing will carry the same weight going forward.
  • Huang's fate will offer an early test, though any decision to reinstate him might reflect investor pressure as much as political influence.

The bottom line: Huang's fate could help establish whether the era of the seemingly untouchable CEO is continuing — or beginning to encounter meaningful limits.
 
 
2. Trump admin moves to close China chip loophole
By Maria Curi
 

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

The Trump administration yesterday released a new rule to close a loophole that allows sensitive U.S. tech to reach China through data centers in the region.

Why it matters: The action comes after mounting pressure on the Commerce Department to block a top U.S. adversary from accessing semiconductors — technology that is central to the AI race.

  • Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with a customer and alleged Chinese spy who works for Megaspeed — a data center company in Singapore — has intensified calls to tackle the diversion of chips to China.

How it works: Before today, it was technically allowed for Chinese firms to access U.S. chips by renting them from data centers in Southeast Asia.

  • The rule targets data centers abroad that supply "significant volumes of computing power" to companies in high-risk countries, including China, Russia and Iran. The data centers have to vet their customers.
  • The regulations, which take effect in 90 days, also require a license to export advanced chips to companies headquartered in countries with high smuggling risk, including Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Brazil.

The intrigue: The interim final rule was released by the Commerce Department but "written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council," a news release states.

  • That language appears to nod to an ongoing and long-standing feud between Commerce Department Secretary Howard Lutnick and other top administration officials including Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.

"One wants to be friendly with China, and one wants to have a blowup with China," President Trump told reporters yesterday, referring to Lutnick and Bessent respectively.

3. Fed warns of AI boom's growing financial risks
By Courtenay Brown and Neil Irwin
 
Note: Survey of 20 market contacts in spring 2026 and 23 in fall 2026; Data: Federal Reserve; Chart: Courtenay Brown

The financial bets underpinning the AI boom are becoming far bigger and harder to untangle than soaring debt figures alone suggest.

  • That is the new warning from the Federal Reserve, which, for the first time, devoted a section to AI financing in its latest assessment of financial stability.

Why it matters: If AI investments fail to generate expected returns, the losses could spread beyond technology companies to the banks and investors financing them.

  • The Fed's warning is not a response to the Nvidia turmoil that has unfolded in recent weeks. The report is published twice a year and largely reflects information available through Oct. 28 — before CEO Jensen Huang's departure.

Driving the news: Fed chairman Kevin Warsh raised the possibility of these risks in opening remarks at a conference yesterday in San Francisco.

  • "In time, the economy would recover, but without the productivity gains," Warsh said in prepared remarks.

By the numbers: The Fed estimates that the largest U.S. banks have nearly $1 trillion in financial exposure to technology companies, data center developers and other businesses and lenders involved in the AI infrastructure boom.

  • Companies borrowed more than $680 billion to finance data centers and other advanced computing infrastructure in the first 10 months of 2026 — roughly five times the amount raised in all of 2023, the Fed says.
  • But other financial commitments have grown even faster: Seven big tech companies — including Nvidia, Microsoft and Oracle — have taken on more than $3 trillion in future lease payments, contracts and financial guarantees.
